(I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "proof_text": "Proof.  We think of the final “blocked’’ configuration as the result of tearing out \(b(n)\) disjoint 3-stamp blocks (each block either 3 in a row or 3 in a column) so that no further 3-stamp block remains.  Call any three consecutive positions in a row or in a column a “potential triple.’’  There are in all  
\[
H \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{horizontal triples,}
\qquad
V \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{vertical triples,}
\]
and hence 
\[
T \;=\;H+V \;=\;2\,n\,(n-2)
\]
potential triples that must each be “hit’’ (i.e.\ each must lose at least one stamp) by our removed blocks.

1.  Lower bound \(b(n)\ge \tfrac1{7}n^2-cn\).  
 
Fix any one of the \(b(n)\) removed blocks.  If it is a horizontal block occupying cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\), then it “hits’’ (i.e.\ destroys at least one cell of) at most
  •  all horizontal triples that include one of those three cells;  in a row of length \(n\), each interior cell lies in 3 horizontal triples and each end‐cell in 1 or 2, and one checks easily that the three consecutive cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\) together lie in at most 5 distinct horizontal triples;

Since in the final configuration every one of the \(T=2n(n-2)\) potential triples must be destroyed by at least one of the removed blocks, and since each block can destroy at most \(14\) triples, we get the inequality
\[
14\,b(n)\;\ge\;2\,n(n-2)\;=\;2n^2-4n,
\]
i.e.
\[
b(n)\;\ge\;\frac{2n^2-4n}{14}
\;=\;\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}\,n.
\]

  B)  A horizontal block in row \(r=4\), columns \(c=3,4,5\).

  C)  A vertical block in column \(c=2\), rows \(r=3,4,5\).

  D)  A vertical block in column \(c=4\), rows \(r=1,2,3\).

  E)  A horizontal block in row \(r=5\), columns \(c=2,3,4\).

Thus after tearing out these \(5\) blocks in each \(5\times5\) cell there is no triple left anywhere in the \(n\times n\) square.

Since there are \(\tfrac n5\) macros in each direction, the total number of blocks used is
\[
5\;\times\;\Bigl(\frac n5\Bigr)^2
\;=\;\frac15\,n^2.
\]
Adding the \(O(n)\) extra blocks needed to cover the final partial strips (of width \(<5\)) along the top and right edges gives
\[
b(n)\;\le\;\frac15\,n^2 \;+\;O(n).
\]
Hence the upper bound holds with some constant \(d\).

Combining (1) and (2) completes the proof: for all \(n>0\),
\[
\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}n\;\le\;b(n)\;\le\;\frac1{5}\,n^2+d\,n,
\]

{"kind":"proof","text":"Take \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).

For the lower bound, assume \(n\ge3\). There are \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and \(n(n-2)\) vertical triples, hence \(2n(n-2)\) potential blocks. In a terminal configuration every such triple contains a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal triples: their starting columns range from two columns before the block to two columns after its start. Each of its three stamps belongs to at most three vertical triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most \(14\) potential triples. The same bound holds for a vertical block. Consequently, if \(m\) blocks have been removed,
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
This applies in particular to \(b(n)\). For \(n=1,2\), we have \(b(n)=0\), and the same inequality still holds.

For the upper bound, first consider the infinite integer grid. In row \(r\), designate the disjoint horizontal blocks
\[
(r,r+5k),\ (r,r+5k+1),\ (r,r+5k+2),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Thus a cell \((r,j)\) is designated precisely when
\[
j-r\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
The undesignated residues are \(3,4\). Hence no three consecutive cells in a row are all undesignated. In a fixed column, as \(r\) increases, \(j-r\pmod5\) runs through consecutive residues in reverse order, so again no three consecutive cells are all undesignated. Therefore every horizontal or vertical triple in the infinite grid meets a designated cell.

Now retain only those designated horizontal blocks lying completely inside the \(n\times n\) sheet, and tear them out. In each row there are at most
\[
\left\lceil\frac{n-2}{5}\right\rceil\le \frac n5+1
\]
such blocks, so initially fewer than or equal to \(n^2/5+n\) blocks are removed.

A designated cell inside the sheet whose designated block was not retained must lie in one of the first two or last two columns. Consequently, every triple surviving the initial removals meets the set \(S\) consisting of those boundary columns, where \(|S|\le4n\). Continue greedily removing any surviving triple until none remains. Every additionally removed triple was already present after the initial removals and therefore contains a cell of \(S\). Since the added blocks are disjoint, there can be at most \(|S|\le4n\) of them.

Thus a terminal configuration is obtained using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Hence
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+5n
\]
for every positive integer \(n\), proving the theorem.","reason":"The supplied lower-bound count is valid, but its proposed \(5\times5\) construction is not: blocks C and E overlap, and row 1, columns 1–3 form an untouched triple. The residue-class construction above supplies disjoint blocks of density \(1/5\), with only \(O(n)\) boundary repairs."}

For the lower bound, suppose first that \(n\ge3\). The sheet contains \(n(n-2)\) horizontal triples and \(n(n-2)\) vertical triples, for a total of \(2n(n-2)\) potential blocks. In any terminal configuration, every such triple contains a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal triples, since the starting position of an intersecting horizontal triple has at most five possibilities. Each of its three stamps belongs to at most three vertical triples, so the block meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus each removed block meets at most \(14\) potential triples; the same argument applies to a vertical block.

Consequently, if \(m\) blocks have been removed in a terminal configuration, then
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
and hence
\[
m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
In particular,
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1,2\), no block can be removed, so \(b(n)=0\), and the same inequality holds.

For the upper bound, first consider the infinite integer grid. In row \(r\), designate the pairwise disjoint horizontal blocks
\[
(r,r+5k),\ (r,r+5k+1),\ (r,r+5k+2),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Thus the cell \((r,j)\) is designated exactly when
\[
j-r\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
The only undesignated residues are \(3,4\), so every three consecutive cells in a row include a designated cell. In a fixed column, as \(r\) increases, \(j-r\pmod5\) runs through consecutive residues in reverse order. Therefore every three consecutive cells in a column also include a designated cell.

Now retain and remove only those designated horizontal blocks lying completely inside the \(n\times n\) sheet. In each row, their number is at most
\[
\left\lceil\frac{n-2}{5}\right\rceil\le \frac n5+1,
\]
so at most \(n^2/5+n\) blocks are initially removed.

If a designated cell lies inside the sheet but its designated block was not retained, then that block crosses the left or right boundary. Hence the cell lies in one of the first two or last two columns. Let \(S\) be the cells in these boundary columns; then \(|S|\le4n\).

Every triple surviving the initial removals contains a designated cell, and that cell cannot belong to a retained block. Thus every surviving triple meets \(S\). Continue greedily removing any surviving triple until none remains. Every additionally removed block contains a cell of \(S\), and these added blocks are pairwise disjoint. Therefore at most \(|S|\le4n\) additional blocks are removed.

This produces a terminal configuration using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Hence, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+5n.
\]
